children.text: Two conducting bodies are immersed in a uniform dielectric, weakly conducting liquid and held at constant voltage difference. Use vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\) and permeability \(\mu_0\) unless stated otherwise. Ignore edge effects for the long cylinders introduced in part 4.
Find the electric field at radial distance \(r\) from an infinite line charge \(\lambda\) in vacuum.

An infinite line at \((x,y)=(-b,0)\) has charge \(+\lambda\), and one at \((b,0)\) has \(-\lambda\). Both are parallel to z. Find potential, setting it to zero at the origin, and sketch equipotential surfaces.

Two identical cylinders have radius \(3a\), length \(l\gg3a\), and axes at \(x=\pm5a,y=0\), parallel to z. A battery holds the left cylinder at higher potential by \(V_0\). Find potential in all regions, zero at the origin.
Find the capacitance of the pair.
Fully immerse both cylinders in liquid of conductivity \(\sigma\) and permittivity \(\epsilon_0\). Find total current between them.
Find resistance of the liquid path.

Find the magnetic field due to the liquid current in part 6, with permeability \(\mu_0\). Use the ideal infinite-length, symmetric current-return model of the source, and explain any angular branch convention.

statement.text:
Conductors in Conducting Liquid
Two conducting bodies are immersed in a uniform dielectric, weakly conducting liquid and held at constant voltage difference. Use vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\) and permeability \(\mu_0\) unless stated otherwise. Ignore edge effects for the long cylinders introduced in part 4.
1. Line-charge field
Find the electric field at radial distance \(r\) from an infinite line charge \(\lambda\) in vacuum.
2. Line-charge potential
Write \(V(r)=f(r)+K\). Find \(f(r)\).
3. Two-line potential and surfaces
An infinite line at \((x,y)=(-b,0)\) has charge \(+\lambda\), and one at \((b,0)\) has \(-\lambda\). Both are parallel to z. Find potential, setting it to zero at the origin, and sketch equipotential surfaces.
4. Conducting-cylinder potential
Two identical cylinders have radius \(3a\), length \(l\gg3a\), and axes at \(x=\pm5a,y=0\), parallel to z. A battery holds the left cylinder at higher potential by \(V_0\). Find potential in all regions, zero at the origin.
5. Cylinder capacitance
Find the capacitance of the pair.
6. Leakage current
Fully immerse both cylinders in liquid of conductivity \(\sigma\) and permittivity \(\epsilon_0\). Find total current between them.
7.R. Pair resistance
Find resistance of the liquid path.
7.RC. Resistance-capacitance product
Find the product RC.
8. Magnetic field
Find the magnetic field due to the liquid current in part 6, with permeability \(\mu_0\). Use the ideal infinite-length, symmetric current-return model of the source, and explain any angular branch convention.

children.text: Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder gives \(\mathbf E=\lambda\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\).
Integrating \(-E_r\) gives \(f(r)=-\lambda\ln(r/r_*)/(2\pi\epsilon_0)\), where any reference length \(r_*\) is absorbed in K. There is no finite choice \(V(\infty)=0\) for an isolated infinite line.

Superposition gives \[V=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac{(x-b)^2+y^2}{(x+b)^2+y^2}.\] Fixed nonzero potential means a fixed ratio of distances, hence coaxial families of circular cylinders parallel to z. The zero-potential surface is the plane \(x=0\).

The appropriate equivalent line charges lie at \(x=\pm4a\). Their distance ratio on each surface is 3 or 1/3, and \(\lambda=\pi\epsilon_0V_0/\ln3\). In the exterior, \[V=\frac{V_0}{4\ln3}\ln\frac{(x-4a)^2+y^2}{(x+4a)^2+y^2}.\] Inside the left cylinder \(V=+V_0/2\), inside the right \(V=-V_0/2\). The line-charge expression must not be continued into the metal.

nodes.alt: Original two-line-charge construction of a cylindrical equipotential surface with distances l1 and l2.

children.text: The charge on the positive cylinder is \(\lambda l\), so \[C=\pi\epsilon_0l/\ln3.\]
The stationary potential obeys the same Laplace problem. Since \(\mathbf j=\sigma\mathbf E\), its flux is \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) times electric displacement flux. Thus \[I=\pi\sigma lV_0/\ln3.\]
Geometry cancels: \(RC=\epsilon_0/\sigma\), the dielectric relaxation time.

Translational symmetry gives an axial field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf z}\). Ampere's law yields \(\partial_yB_z=\mu_0j_x\) and \(\partial_xB_z=-\mu_0j_y\). In the central strip \(|x|<a\), with the source's symmetry \(B_z(x,0)=0\), \[B_z=\frac{\mu_0\sigma V_0}{2\ln3}\left[\arctan\frac y{4a+x}+\arctan\frac y{4a-x}\right].\] A rectangular Ampere loop symmetric about \(y=0\) gives the same result by integrating \(j_x\) across it. Away from this strip, continue the angular functions on the appropriate exterior branches rather than blindly using principal arctangents. A physical finite cylinder and its battery leads require the return-current geometry, omitted by the ideal edge-free model. The source's unqualified principal-arctangent formula is therefore used only in its valid central region here.

nodes.alt: Original current flow between cylinders and rectangular Ampere loop used to find the axial magnetic field.

solution.text:
Conductors in Conducting Liquid
1. Line-charge field
Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder gives \(\mathbf E=\lambda\hat{\mathbf r}/(2\pi\epsilon_0r)\).
2. Line-charge potential
Integrating \(-E_r\) gives \(f(r)=-\lambda\ln(r/r_*)/(2\pi\epsilon_0)\), where any reference length \(r_*\) is absorbed in K. There is no finite choice \(V(\infty)=0\) for an isolated infinite line.
3. Two-line potential and surfaces
Superposition gives \[V=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\ln\frac{(x-b)^2+y^2}{(x+b)^2+y^2}.\] Fixed nonzero potential means a fixed ratio of distances, hence coaxial families of circular cylinders parallel to z. The zero-potential surface is the plane \(x=0\).
4. Conducting-cylinder potential
The appropriate equivalent line charges lie at \(x=\pm4a\). Their distance ratio on each surface is 3 or 1/3, and \(\lambda=\pi\epsilon_0V_0/\ln3\). In the exterior, \[V=\frac{V_0}{4\ln3}\ln\frac{(x-4a)^2+y^2}{(x+4a)^2+y^2}.\] Inside the left cylinder \(V=+V_0/2\), inside the right \(V=-V_0/2\). The line-charge expression must not be continued into the metal.

5. Cylinder capacitance
The charge on the positive cylinder is \(\lambda l\), so \[C=\pi\epsilon_0l/\ln3.\]
6. Leakage current
The stationary potential obeys the same Laplace problem. Since \(\mathbf j=\sigma\mathbf E\), its flux is \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) times electric displacement flux. Thus \[I=\pi\sigma lV_0/\ln3.\]
7.R. Pair resistance
\(R=V_0/I=\ln3/(\pi\sigma l)\).
7.RC. Resistance-capacitance product
Geometry cancels: \(RC=\epsilon_0/\sigma\), the dielectric relaxation time.
8. Magnetic field
Translational symmetry gives an axial field \(\mathbf B=B_z\hat{\mathbf z}\). Ampere's law yields \(\partial_yB_z=\mu_0j_x\) and \(\partial_xB_z=-\mu_0j_y\). In the central strip \(|x|<a\), with the source's symmetry \(B_z(x,0)=0\), \[B_z=\frac{\mu_0\sigma V_0}{2\ln3}\left[\arctan\frac y{4a+x}+\arctan\frac y{4a-x}\right].\] A rectangular Ampere loop symmetric about \(y=0\) gives the same result by integrating \(j_x\) across it. Away from this strip, continue the angular functions on the appropriate exterior branches rather than blindly using principal arctangents. A physical finite cylinder and its battery leads require the return-current geometry, omitted by the ideal edge-free model. The source's unqualified principal-arctangent formula is therefore used only in its valid central region here.
